subject: Compilers
title: Compilers: Principles & Tools
subtitle: Syntax Analysis, Code Gen & Optimization
author: Alfred V. Aho, Monica S. Lam, Ravi Sethi & Jeffrey D. Ullman

pages.title: The Structure of a Modern Compiler
bulletPoints: Analysis-Synthesis Model: Front-end analyzes source language; Back-end synthesizes target machine code.
Linear phases: Lexical Analysis -> Syntax Analysis -> Semantic Analysis -> Intermediate Code -> Optimization -> Code Gen.
Symbol Table Manager: Maintains identifiers, scoping levels, type attributes, memory offsets, and function signatures.
Error Handler: Detecting, reporting, and recovering from syntax and semantic errors to continue compilation.

pages.title: Lexical Analysis & Tokenization
bulletPoints: Role of the Lexer: Converting raw character streams into meaningful lexical tokens <token-name, attribute-value>.
Patterns and Lexemes: The character sequence matching a token pattern (e.g. 'while' matching KEYWORD).
Handling whitespace and comments: Stripping comments and whitespace without altering source line number tracking.
Buffer pairs: Using two N-character buffers and forward/lexeme-beginning pointers to avoid costly single-character disk reads.

pages.title: Regular Expressions & Language Specification
bulletPoints: Formal languages: Alphabets (Sigma), strings, concatenation, alternation (|), Kleene closure (*), positive closure (+).
Regular definitions: Giving names to regular expressions for programming tokens (digits, letters, identifiers, numbers).
Extensions: Character classes [a-z], optional elements (?), and word boundary anchors.
Limitations: Why regular expressions cannot describe nested balanced parentheses or recursive structures (Chomsky hierarchy).

pages.title: Finite Automata: NFA and DFA
bulletPoints: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA): Exactly one transition state per input character; no epsilon transitions.
Nondeterministic Finite Automata (NFA): Multiple transitions possible on the same symbol, plus epsilon (empty) moves.
Thompson's Construction: Algorithm converting arbitrary regular expressions into equivalent NFAs in O(n) time.
Subset Construction Algorithm: Converting NFAs into minimal deterministic DFAs using epsilon-closure sets.

pages.title: DFA State Minimization & Lexer Generators
bulletPoints: Hopcroft's DFA Minimization: Partitioning states into distinguishable groups to produce the unique minimal-state DFA.
Lookahead ambiguities: Resolving longest-match rule (e.g. '==' vs '=') and rule priority order.
Lex and Flex tools: Translating regular expression specifications into compact C/C++ lexer transition tables.
Direct-coded lexers: Hand-written switch-case lexers achieving maximum throughput in production compilers.

pages.title: Context-Free Grammars & Syntax Trees
bulletPoints: Context-Free Grammar (CFG): Four-tuple G = (V_N, V_T, P, S) defining recursive syntactic structure.
Derivations: Leftmost and rightmost derivations replacing non-terminals with production right-hand sides.
Parse Trees: Graphical representations of grammatical derivations showing hierarchical sentence structure.
Ambiguity in grammars: Multiple parse trees for single expressions (e.g. the dangling-else problem) and disambiguation rules.

pages.title: Top-Down Parsing & Recursive Descent
bulletPoints: Top-down parsing strategy: Constructing parse tree from root (Start symbol) downward to leaves (terminals).
Backtracking recursive descent: Predictive parsing vs backtracking overhead and infinite loops on left recursion.
Eliminating left recursion: Rewriting A -> A alpha | beta into A -> beta A' and A' -> alpha A' | epsilon.
Left factoring: Factoring out common prefixes to enable deterministic single-token lookahead parsing.

pages.title: LL(1) Predictive Parsing
bulletPoints: FIRST and FOLLOW sets: Mathematical construction of token lookahead sets for production selection.
LL(1) Grammars: Left-to-right scan, Leftmost derivation, 1-token lookahead; grammar has no parsing table conflicts.
Parsing table construction: Mapping non-terminal A and lookahead token 'a' to a unique production rule.
Non-recursive predictive parsing: Explicit parsing stack and input buffer driven by LL(1) transition matrix.

pages.title: Bottom-Up Parsing: Shift-Reduce Concept
bulletPoints: Bottom-up strategy: Constructing parse tree from terminal leaves upward to the root start symbol.
Handle pruning: Identifying substrings matching production right-hand sides and reducing them to non-terminals.
Shift-Reduce parser states: Shift (push token onto stack), Reduce (replace handle with non-terminal), Accept, Error.
Conflicts: Shift/Reduce conflicts and Reduce/Reduce conflicts arising from ambiguous or un-parseable grammars.

pages.title: LR(0) and SLR(1) Parsing
bulletPoints: LR Parser architecture: Input buffer, parsing stack of (state, symbol) pairs, and Action/Goto parsing tables.
LR(0) items: Productions with dot markers indicating parser progress (e.g. A -> alpha . beta).
Canonical collection of LR(0) items: Using closure and GOTO operations to build DFA of parser states.
Simple LR (SLR(1)): Using FOLLOW sets of non-terminals to resolve reduce actions and eliminate shift/reduce conflicts.

pages.title: Canonical LR(1) and LALR(1) Parsers
bulletPoints: LR(1) items: Enhancing LR(0) items with explicit lookahead tokens [A -> alpha . beta, a].
Canonical LR(1) tables: Extremely powerful, accepting all deterministic context-free languages, but with thousands of states.
LALR(1) (Look-Ahead LR): Merging states with identical core LR(0) items, reducing table size to SLR(1) proportions.
Yacc and Bison: Industry-standard LALR(1) parser generators generating C code from grammar rules.

pages.title: Syntax-Directed Translation (SDT)
bulletPoints: Syntax-Directed Definitions (SDD): Associating semantic attributes and semantic rules with grammar productions.
Synthesized attributes: Computed from child node attributes in the parse tree (bottom-up evaluation).
Inherited attributes: Computed from parent or sibling node attributes (top-down context propagation).
S-Attributed and L-Attributed definitions: Ensuring semantic actions can be evaluated during standard LR parsing.

pages.title: Abstract Syntax Trees (AST)
bulletPoints: Parse Tree vs Abstract Syntax Tree: Dropping syntactic punctuation, retaining only operators and semantic operands.
Node representations: Discriminated unions / class hierarchies for Expressions, Statements, Declarations, and Blocks.
Homogeneous vs Heterogeneous ASTs: General node types vs strictly-typed language-specific AST structures.
Visitor Pattern: Traversing AST nodes cleanly to perform type checking, interpretation, and code generation.

pages.title: Semantic Analysis & Type Checking
bulletPoints: Type systems: Primitive types, compound types (arrays, structs, pointers), function types, and subtyping.
Static vs dynamic typing: Catching type errors at compile time vs checking type tags at runtime.
Type checking rules: Semantic validation of assignments, function parameter compatibility, and implicit coercions.
Scope resolution: Lexical scoping rules, shadowing, symbol table enter/exit scopes, and forward declarations.

pages.title: Intermediate Representations (IR)
bulletPoints: Why Intermediate Representations matter: Decoupling M source front-ends from N target machine architectures (M + N vs M × N).
Three-Address Code (TAC): Linear quadruples (op, arg1, arg2, result) where each instruction has at most three operands.
Static Single Assignment (SSA) form: Every variable is assigned exactly once; phi-nodes resolve diverging control paths.
High-level vs Low-level IR: High-level ASTs preserve language semantics; Low-level IR mirrors target machine registers.

pages.title: Control Flow Graphs & Basic Blocks
bulletPoints: Basic Block: A sequence of consecutive intermediate instructions with single entry and single exit.
Leader identification: Target of jumps, instructions immediately following jumps, and program entry points.
Control Flow Graph (CFG): Directed graph where nodes are basic blocks and edges represent branch and jump paths.
Dominator trees: Node D dominates node N if every execution path from entry to N must pass through D.

pages.title: Data-Flow Analysis & Liveness
bulletPoints: Data-flow frameworks: Computing program properties over CFGs using iterative transfer functions and meet operators.
Reaching Definitions: Determining which variable definitions may reach a given program point.
Live-Variable Analysis: Backward data-flow analysis finding which variables hold values that may be read in future steps.
Available Expressions: Forward data-flow analysis eliminating redundant re-computations of common subexpressions.

pages.title: Classical Machine-Independent Optimizations
bulletPoints: Common Subexpression Elimination (CSE): Reusing previously computed expressions stored in temporary variables.
Constant Folding and Constant Propagation: Evaluating compile-time constants and propagating known values.
Dead Code Elimination: Deleting unreachable basic blocks and computations whose results are never read.
Copy Propagation: Replacing occurrences of variable y with x after assignment y = x.

pages.title: Loop Optimizations & Vectorization
bulletPoints: Loop Invariant Code Motion (Hoisting): Moving calculations whose values do not change outside the loop pre-header.
Strength Reduction: Replacing expensive operations (e.g. multiplication inside loops) with cheaper ones (addition).
Loop Unrolling: Duplicating loop bodies to reduce branch overhead and expose instruction-level parallelism.
Auto-vectorization: Transforming scalar loops into parallel SIMD instructions (AVX, NEON) over array elements.

pages.title: Run-Time Memory Environments & Stack Frames
bulletPoints: Process memory layout: Code segment, Static data, Heap (dynamic allocation), and Call Stack.
Stack Activation Records (Frames): Return address, previous frame pointer (EBP/RBP), saved registers, local variables.
Calling conventions: cdecl, System V AMD64 ABI, Microsoft x64 (argument passing in registers vs stack).
Access links and display arrays: Supporting nested functions and static closures in block-structured languages.

pages.title: Heap Management & Garbage Collection
bulletPoints: Dynamic memory allocation: Explicit malloc/free management vs automatic runtime garbage collection.
Reference Counting: Tracking reference tallies; immediate reclamation but unable to collect cyclic pointer structures.
Tracing Garbage Collection: Mark-and-Sweep from root sets (stack, globals) followed by sweep of unreachable heap cells.
Generational GC: The weak generational hypothesis; separating young eden spaces from old survivor tenures.

pages.title: Register Allocation via Graph Coloring
bulletPoints: The Register Allocation problem: Mapping an unbounded number of IR variables to K physical hardware registers.
Interference Graphs: Nodes are variable live ranges; edges connect variables that are simultaneously live.
Chaitin-Briggs Graph Coloring: K-coloring the interference graph in polynomial time using Kempe heuristics.
Spilling: When a graph cannot be K-colored, selecting candidate variables to spill into memory stack slots.

pages.title: Instruction Selection & Code Generation
bulletPoints: Target machine architectures: RISC (fixed-width, load/store) vs CISC (variable-length, memory operands).
Tree Rewriting & Maximal Munch: Tiling AST expression trees with target machine instruction templates.
Dynamic programming for instruction selection: Finding optimal instruction sequences with minimum cycle cost.
Peephole Optimization: Sliding small window over generated machine code to eliminate redundant loads and jumps.

pages.title: Instruction Scheduling & Pipeline Hazards
bulletPoints: Instruction Scheduling: Reordering machine instructions to avoid hardware pipeline stalls without altering program semantics.
Dependency graphs: Read-After-Write (RAW), Write-After-Read (WAR), and Write-After-Write (WAW) latency edges.
List scheduling algorithm: Prioritizing critical path instructions on ready queues to minimize total cycle time.
VLIW and EPIC architectures: Compiler-directed parallel instruction issue and software pipelining.

pages.title: Modern Compilers: LLVM, JIT, and Synthesis
bulletPoints: The LLVM Compiler Infrastructure: Universal typed SSA intermediate representation and modular optimizer passes.
Just-In-Time (JIT) Compilation: Compiling hot bytecode loops into native machine code at runtime (V8, JVM HotSpot).
Profile-Guided Optimization (PGO): Using actual execution telemetry to optimize branch predictions and inline functions.
Compiler verification and formal methods: CompCert formally verified C compiler and the future of language engineering.
